memories.memory_text: I remember leaning back in my chair, steepling my fingers, and telling Rex to tell me his troubles — it was the moment he officially became my client, and I could already see this wasn't just about divorce, it was about domination.
I told Ken my client got absolutely nothing—zero, zip—and he didn’t need to worry about seeing her for surgery, not unless her HMO covered it, which it didn’t.

I looked at the LeCoultre Revers he gave me, flipped it in my hand, and thought about how we used to talk about clerking for the Supreme Court—now I’m here, in Beverly Hills, getting watches and Botox pitches instead.

I took Herb's withered hand in the dim light, feeling the clamminess of his skin and the rope-like veins beneath, and when he called me the engine that drives this firm, all I could manage was a quiet 'Thank you, Herb'—it was acknowledgment, not just of work, but of succession.

I was adjusting my smile in the mirror, rehearsing a greeting for Marylin—something smooth, professional—when the door opened and she was standing there with him, that oilman Doyle, and I couldn’t stop the ‘who the fuck are you’ from slipping out.
Doyle called Marylin 'baby' and told her to go first, then sat next to her on the couch. I invited them in.
I remember snapping at Wrigley, asking what the hell was wrong with him—sniffling like some sentimental fool while we sat through another predictable wedding charade.

I remember wondering if she was actually going to go through with it—Marylin standing there in that simple gown, seconds from sealing her fate while the rabbi droned on about marriage as some kind of recipe.
I reached across the table and took her hand after she accused me of thinking she had no soul—she let me hold it, and I just stroked it, quietly, while the waiter stood there with the menu.

I was standing there in the storm, gun in hand, pulling the trigger—Bonnie fell, then Mrs. Guttman, and when I turned to Marilyn, I hesitated… then a voice kept rasping, 'Counseluh? Counseluh?' like an accusation.

I woke up drenched in sweat, the phone ringing—Marilyn on the line, slurring, saying she was worthless, that she sucked, screaming at someone, driving on Sunset… and I told her to come straight to me, not to stop anywhere.
I told Marylin my mother never particularly cared for me — that I wasn’t her 'type,' just a difficult baby she never recovered from.
I held her hand when she went to leave, told her not to go, and kissed her — and she kissed me back.
I fumbled the words at first—said 'I want to be your wife'—but I caught it, looked her in the eye, and asked her to marry me, truly meaning it for the first time in my life.
After she said yes, I panicked for a second—I didn't have a ring, just my watch—and I remember her laughing, kissing me, like it didn't matter at all.
I stood in the chapel, nervous, waiting for Wrigley. I asked if he had it — the Massey Pre-nup. I confirmed he had the pre-nup, not Kenneth.

When Marylin walked in—radiant, real, flanked by her friends—I suddenly wasn't sure if the document in that briefcase could protect me from what I actually feared: letting go of my armor and facing love without terms.

I blurted out 'I do' too soon, before the judge could even finish the question — I could feel Marylin's glare and the judge's irritation, like I was some nervous rookie at a wedding instead of a man who's spent his life controlling every word.
After staring at my shoes for a long moment, I finally said 'I do' again — this time slow and sure, like I was stepping off a ledge I'd spent my whole life avoiding.

I woke up and kissed Marylin good morning before getting dressed for work. She brought me coffee, and I held up two ties—she picked one, and we both laughed over breakfast with the fruit and those silly Wrigley spoons.

I came home and Marylin greeted me at the door. I changed into casual clothes while telling her about my day. We had a candlelit dinner with fish, pasta, and tulips on the table. Later, we sat on the couch watching Seinfeld. Before bed, we lay in bed looking at each other as the lights went out.
For the first time, I stood before my associates and admitted I was in love—truly in love—calling it the seed of my livelihood, ironic as that once frightened me.
I asked the room whether we should extinguish our clients' dying flames of love or fan them back to life, knowing my own choice—to build, to trust, to practice law with love—had already been made.

I told Marylin to go out and buy woman things, personal touches — to Marylinize the house. I handed her my card and said to spend as much as she wanted, that this place needed to stop being a bachelor pad and become a married house.

I brought up the room off the bedroom — said it could be a nursery someday. I took her hands and mentioned taking out the refrigeration unit from the humidor, but she kissed me before I could finish. I remember asking if she wanted children.
A woman suddenly confronted me outside the flower store, accusing me of ruining her life and snatching the bouquet I'd just bought—then she started eating a rose petal like it meant something.

She said Howard Doyle was her brother and that my marriage to Marylin was a setup—phony wife, fake pre-nup—orchestrated as revenge, and she laughed while singing 'neener neener neener' like it was all a joke.

I remember standing in Ruth's office, the weight of it hitting me — I didn't have a pre-nup, and Marylin must have known all along. I could feel my control slipping, my voice breaking as I asked, 'Why did she do it, Ruth? Why?'
I walked in and saw the house completely changed—antiques, rugs, a Biedermeyer couch—everything I didn’t ask for, didn’t want, suddenly there, like my space had been erased.
I asked her if she could return the trust, the hopes, the dreams—bitterly, like it was all just something bought and returnable, because in that moment, love felt like a transaction she could undo.

I left the note on the pillow, the Shakespeare line—'If you wrong us, shall we not revenge?'—and walked out without looking back. I don’t know if she read it, but it was the last thing I owed her: clarity.
I already made my move, Kenneth — and there's no taking it back, not in court and not with Marylin.
She stood there chewing on a cigar like she owned the place, telling me she was reporting me to the IRS — not about money, but the 'stuff,' the gifts from clients I never declared.
The way she looked at my watch and asked 'what time' — it wasn't casual, it felt like she was measuring how much I had to lose, like she already knew the next move was coming.
I heard Marylin say she fell in love with me, and for the first time, I didn’t calculate or deflect — I just said it back: 'So did I.'
I kept telling her to leave the house, urgency in my voice, because I knew something was wrong — then I heard a car screech outside, and I knew it was too late.
I whispered 'Marylin?' as I crept into the dark foyer, thinking I was alone—then saw Joe in the kitchen, and for a second, I thought he was here to help.
When she said 'It's a no go, Joe,' and he kept unscrewing the silencer, I realized she was the one who hired him—and then I saw her look at me like it was all my fault.
I told her that something inside me died when I found out she'd hired someone to kill me — but then she threw it back in my face, and I could see the damage was already beyond repair.
I pulled out the postnup, signed it right there, and pushed it across the table — she just looked at me, then tore it in half without a word.
I held that box of Pre-Castro Cohibas, feeling the weight of them—not just the cigars, but what they stood for. For a second, I let myself remember the man I used to be.
I tossed the box to the construction worker—'Here, buddy. These are for you.' It wasn’t just cigars I was giving up. It was the old life, the old version of me.

memories.memory_text: I tried the key, and it didn’t work — I rattled the knob, pressed the bell, called out… and then her voice came through the intercom, cold, telling me to get away from the door. I just wanted to talk, to explain… but she wouldn’t even let me in.

I sat there, nervous, trying to explain about Marylin—how it wasn’t that things cooled down, not exactly, and how she’s still a knock-out, very sexy—but I couldn’t even finish the thought, my voice just trailing off, hands probably shaking.

I remember hearing my name, Miles Massey, spoken like it meant something — but I wasn’t there, not really, just the weight of it hanging in the air, and the way Marylin said it so calm, like she already knew what it would cost.
I heard they bought her speech—Pat wouldn’t testify. I didn’t do anything wrong, but if that’s what it took to keep things from falling apart, then… it had to be done. I can’t lose everything.
I felt the old man's hand—cold, veined, so dry and clammy—when he reached out, and I had to take it, even though I didn't want to. I just stood there, shaking it, not knowing what else to do.
I was on the little train, singing 'Casey Jones'—my voice cracking—those women pushing me, laughing, their hands on the rails, and I couldn’t tell if it was funny or if I was supposed to stop.
I heard the pilots talking—'Rex Rexroth, the mini-mall king'—and then 'buying Indiana'—I didn’t say anything, just kept facing forward, my hands tight on the toy train.

I heard they were talking about Marylin—divorced now, and rich, really rich—like, Croesus-level. I don’t know how I feel about it, but it’s out there, and people are already using her name like it’s a deal.
I sent Miles those cigars... two humidors, pre-Castro. I thought it might help keep things smooth, you know? Just in case he ever talked to Marylin.
They said my name—Hamilton-Rexroth—like it was part of some legal formula, something signed and sealed, and I wasn’t even there… but it still made my stomach twist.
Marylin said I was married before her.
I heard they used my name—something about Marylin, my wife, and that deal going south... I don’t know how much is true, but if it’s out there, people talking, then it’s bad—really bad.
I was singing, trying to keep it light, surrounded by the girls, the film playing on the wall — and then this pain shot through my arm, I couldn't hide it, I just bent over, couldn't speak...
Rex is dead. I remember the phone call — Marvin Untermeyer’s voice, flat, saying it like it was just business. No warning. Just... he’s gone.
Everything goes to Marylin. And I’m still married to her — no prenup. I remember the weight of it hitting me, sitting there in the dark, thinking — I’m tied to this. What have I done?

I remember saying 'Murder!' when Marylin brought up Rex Rexroth—my voice cracked, my hands were shaking, and I could feel the blood in my temples. It wasn't just anger, it was fear—like everything was unraveling again.
